past_actions.summary: Spend two weeks systematically talking to the professional mechanics and small independent shops in the region — find out what they're actually struggling to source, what their lead times look like from existing suppliers, and whether any of them feel underserved by the big distributors.
past_actions.emotional_state: Controlled unease. Not panicking — the savings buffer and positive monthly flow keep the immediate fear muted. But I'm not comfortable either. There's a background anxiety that has been present for a couple years now, a low-grade awareness that I'm watching the ground erode under something I built. The feeling isn't paralyzing; it's clarifying. I've been too patient. Time to move.

past_actions.summary: Begin liquidating the bottom-performing 20% of DIY-specific SKUs — clearance pricing to move them out, freeing up roughly $4,000-6,000 in shelf space and working capital. Immediately redirect that freed capital toward restocking the professional-grade lines where mechanics have been telling me they face lead-time delays: brake hardware, specialty gaskets, import vehicle sensors.
past_actions.emotional_state: Cautiously encouraged. The savings bump feels like confirmation that the outreach wasn't just time spent — it's starting to convert. But Tamika's closure is a gut-punch reminder that eleven months of runway is not safety, it's borrowed time with interest. I'm moving faster than I was at T0, but the underlying anxiety hasn't lifted. Two dependents. A mortgage with 46 months left. These aren't abstractions. I keep the pressure on myself on purpose.

past_actions.summary: Have a direct conversation with Carlos Ruiz about his EV retraining — specifically ask what parts and consumables the shop is going to need as they take on more EV and hybrid work. Frame it as a business question, not small talk: what do they currently source, where from, what's hard to get, what lead times look like for ADAS sensors, high-voltage safety gear, EV battery diagnostic tools. This is a customer discovery call disguised as a relationship maintenance call.
past_actions.emotional_state: More clear-eyed than last tick, and slightly unsettled by my own clarity. The savings bump was encouraging and I let it feel like confirmation when it might just be lag — the old customers responding to the new inventory, before the deeper shift shows up in the numbers. I'm not panicking. But I'm not letting myself feel good about eleven months of runway either. Two kids, a mortgage in its last years, and a business in a sector that every institutional signal says is contracting. The right feeling is alert, not anxious.

past_actions.summary: Draft and send a formal letter of interest to RoboRide's regional fleet operations manager identifying Howard's Parts as a potential parts supplier for their Millfield vehicle maintenance. Include a preliminary capability list covering brake hardware, sensors, lubricants, and safety consumables that fleet maintenance requires. Also reach out to the local municipality's vehicle maintenance department — garbage trucks, transit buses, city fleet — with the same pitch. This is a cold outreach to B2B customers that don't know me yet.

Follow up by phone with RoboRide's regional fleet operations contact — a brief, professional call to confirm receipt of the letter of interest from last tick, ask about their maintenance sourcing timeline, and offer to provide a sample order of brake consumables at cost as a relationship-builder. Simultaneously, follow up with the municipality vehicle maintenance department to see if the letter landed with the right person.

Re-approach RoboRide regional fleet operations with a specific, numbers-forward pitch now that their Millfield expansion is publicly announced. Howard drafts a one-page capabilities summary — not a letter of interest, a vendor proposal — that lists his current inventory of brake consumables, filters, lubricants, and sensors with unit pricing and next-day local delivery capacity. He calls the regional fleet ops contact, references the prior outreach, and frames the timing explicitly: 'You just announced residential expansion and a delivery partnership. That means more vehicles running more miles in this zip code. I am ten minutes from your nearest maintenance lot and I can have brake pads on their bench by tomorrow morning.' The goal is a trial order or a meeting with their fleet maintenance supervisor. This is the highest-leverage move available given the timing of their expansion announcement.

reflections.reflection: Six ticks in and the shape of this thing is becoming clearer. The DIY market is shrinking faster than I projected two years ago — robotaxis now at 7% adoption in Millfield, sector revenue index at 79. Patricia Hawkins laying off people she personally knew at the dealership is the loudest signal yet that no one in auto retail is insulated just by being established. My pivot toward B2B and commercial fleet accounts is the right direction. The letter to RoboRide, the municipality outreach, the brake consumable sample — those were all correct moves. But they cost money and haven't converted yet. I need to hold steady without bleeding out. The EV retraining happening with Carlos and Sarah is a real opportunity: if I can become their go-to local supplier for EV and hybrid parts before they cement supplier relationships with the big distributors, that is durable revenue in a growing segment. This tick is about consolidation, not expansion. Build the tools, deepen the relationships, spend nothing.
reflections.identity_shift: I am moving from 'store owner in a shrinking market' toward 'commercial parts supplier for a transitioning auto ecosystem.' The identity isn't fully formed yet, but the direction is clear. The skills I have — automotive knowledge, local relationships, small business operations — are still relevant in the B2B lane even if they are fading in the DIY lane. The shift feels less frightening than it did at tick 0. It feels more like a choice I am making rather than a thing being done to me.
regrets: I ran a tick 3 routine without clear action. That was a wasted tick. The sector was already showing stress signals and I coasted. I will not do that again.
I should have begun the EV parts inventory build-out even earlier. The window when I could have been the obvious local EV parts source before competitors noticed is narrowing.
successes: The shift from DIY SKU inventory to professional-grade lines (brake hardware, specialty gaskets, import sensors) is showing in the savings trajectory — modest positive flow through ticks 0-3.
The cold B2B outreach to RoboRide and the municipality was the right instinct, even if it hasn't converted yet. I planted seeds in two channels that could be transformative if even one converts.
The Carlos Ruiz customer discovery call at tick 2 was excellent intelligence-gathering that I am now building on. That relationship is real.
reflections.adaptation_notes: The commercial capability sheet I am drafting this tick is a leverage tool — it converts future conversations from exploratory to operational. When RoboRide or the municipality asks what I can supply, I need to answer with a document, not a story. Carlos and Sarah are the bridge between my existing inventory pivot and the EV future. If I can serve two mechanics who are actively transitioning, I am inside the EV maintenance ecosystem before it fully forms. That is where I want to be.
